Egypt’s president is waiting for parliament to formally approve the deployment of troops to Saudi Arabia after it delayed a vote on the matter for a week amid opposition concerns that it could drag Cairo into a [regional quagmire](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76474).
Lawmakers have until October 26 to debate, and are expected to raise questions about the scope of the mission, the risks Egyptian troops might face, and whether the deployment could escalate into direct fighting with the Houthis.
 
Publicly, no indication has been given on the number of troops Egypt may send. Reports indicate the deployment would prominently feature air defense and logistical support, including protection of Saudi airports and oil infrastructure.
 
The question of potential direct fighting with Yemenis is a central one:
 
🔶 In November, Egypt will mark the 59th anniversary of its withdrawal from Yemen in 1967 after a five-year mission which drained the nation’s coffers and killed or injured up to 40k troops in grueling guerrilla warfare against the barefooted Zaydi royalist tribesmen of northern Yemen.
 
🔶 Described by historians as “Egypt’s Vietnam,” the campaign saw Egyptian troops face off against the direct tribal and religious ancestors of today’s Houthis (who, in a twist of history, were being backed by Saudi Arabia, Britain, Israel and Iran at the time to stop the spread of Egypt’s [pan-Arab nationalist ideology](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/76556)).

🔶 Egypt’s defeat in Yemen left its military exhausted, weakened and demoralized ahead of Israel’s June 1967 surprise assault, which would reshape the region for [decades](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/60424) to come.
🔶 Fast forward to the present, and the modern successors to the Zaydi tribesmen are not only politically far stronger and more organized, but possess missiles and drones that could reach Egypt itself.
